title: Sherry trades O’s job for Ag job, a shakeup at top of Moore reelection campaign, in political notes
summary: Nicole Sherry trades her job as the Baltimore Orioles' head groundskeeper for a job as a state bureaucrat -- and is actually excited by the move -- while Ron Owens abruptly "steps away" from his job running the governor's reelection campaign, in political notes.
content:
by Christine Condon and Steve Crane, Maryland Matters May 15, 2026

by Christine Condon and Steve Crane, Maryland Matters May 15, 2026

Baltimore Orioles head groundskeeper Nicole Sherry is heading from the Yard to the state capital.

After 23 years with the Major League Baseball team, Sherry was named an assistant secretary at the Maryland Department of Agriculture earlier this week. Her last game manicuring the grasses of Camden Yards was Tuesday.

“We couldn’t be more excited to welcome Nicole,” Maryland Agriculture Secretary Kevin Atticks said in a news release. “Her experience managing complex operations and leading teams, combined with her strong agricultural background and proven leadership, will be an incredible asset to MDA.”

Sherry will serve as assistant secretary of plant industries and pest management, according to a news release from the department, overseeing pesticide regulation, mosquito control, plant protection, turf and seed regulation and the Office of the State Chemist.

Sherry was named head groundskeeper for the Orioles in 2006, becoming only the second woman ever to hold the role for a Major League team. She was promoted to director of field operations in 2021 and senior director of field operations in 2023.

But Sherry, who received an agriculture degree from the University of Delaware, said the post with the state’s agricultural agency was a natural fit.

“Agriculture has always been my passion and I’m looking forward to joining the Maryland Department of Agriculture and working with communities across the state,” she said in the news release. “I am excited to join the Plant Industries and Pest Management teams and work alongside such incredibly smart and dedicated individuals.”

The manager of Gov. Wes Moore’s reelection campaign is “stepping away” from the job and will be replaced by a member of Moore’s administration.

Ron Owens’ last day is Friday and he will be replaced on Monday by Dylan Arant, who currently reports to Moore’s chief of staff, Lester Davis. The sudden shift comes a little more than six weeks before the June 23 primary and just 10 days after Moore’s formal kickoff of his reelection campaign. It also comes a week after Moore released a list of more than 160 endorsements that was as notable for the candidates endorsed as it was for the high-profile Democrats snubbed, including Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) and Del. Aletheia McCaskill (D-Baltimore County).

In a statement, the Moore campaign gave no reason for the change, except to say that with governor in “a strong position to win in November, Ron Owens will be stepping away as campaign manager,”

“Ron has been an invaluable part of Wes Moore’s re-election campaign,” campaign spokesperson Carter Elliott IV said in a statement. “His dedication, hard work and commitment … have helped us build the strong foundation the campaign stands on today and we are grateful for everything he has contributed.”

Moore officially launches reelection bid with Baltimore, Prince George’s events

Arant “will assume leadership of the campaign as campaign manager” effective Monday, the statement said. Before working in Moore’s office, Arant worked on the campaigns of Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown and North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, for whom he was chief of staff when Jackson served in the 118th Congress.

Moore tapped Owens last summer. Though he was only 29 at the time, Owens was already a seasoned political operative who had worked as a campaign adviser to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, among other jobs. Most of his experience, however, was in his native Michigan, where he worked on the 2018 and 2022 campaigns of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. His hire by Moore raised some eyebrows at the time since Whitmer, like Moore, is one of the Democratic governors often mentioned as a potential presidential candidate in 2028.

Before 2028, however, Moore has to win reelection. Despite softening favorability numbers in recent polls, the race is largely seen as Moore’s — and, now, Arant’s — to lose: The governor has high name recognition, a reported $8 million in the bank and the power of incumbency. He faces just one challenger in the Democratic primary, Eric Felber, while the Republicans have a nine-way primary battle that was deprived of its biggest name when former Gov. Larry Hogan announced in January that he would not run again.
